stem: 28-year-old female presented with severe epigastric pain and epigastric tenderness, labs revealed amylase 1253 UI and normal LFTs + multiple gallstones in US and mild intrahepatic biliary dilatation. After 3 days the patient improved clinically and amylase returned to the normal level. What is the next appropriate management?
srcNote: (Pancreas) Source note (Final 433 A Q6 (p. 177)): Cholecystectomy at the same admission to not have another attack of pancreatitis. Source note (Final 437 A Q57): The related recall after ERCP with sphincterotomy and common bile duct stone clearance gives D. Cholecystectomy during the index admission. Ans. D.
expl: Mild gallstone pancreatitis (normal LFTs, stone passed) → cholecystectomy during the same admission once settled — waiting 6–8 weeks risks recurrence (~30%).

why.D: ERCP only for retained CBD stone/cholangitis.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain. On examination, he is febrile and tachycardic, with tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory tests show elevated bilirubin and cholestatic liver enzymes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: (Biliary Tract)
expl: Fever + jaundice + RUQ pain (Charcot's triad) with cholestatic LFTs = acute (ascending) cholangitis.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with right upper quadrant pain and fever. Ultrasound shows a dilated gallbladder with pericholecystic fluid, and she has a positive Murphy’s sign. What is the most appropriate management?
srcNote: (Biliary Tract) The retained source gives index-admission cholecystectomy. A related 438 F recall accepts two options, reproduced below. Other source key (Final 438 F Q35): B. Cholecystectomy after subsided her symptoms; C. Urgent cholecystectomy. B/C.
expl: Acute calculous cholecystitis → early laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the index admission (within ~72 h–1 week) — fewer readmissions, same complication rate. A related 438 recall noted the early window.

stem: What is a key clinical sign indicating inflammation of the gallbladder?
expl: Murphy's sign — inspiratory arrest on palpation of the RUQ — indicates gallbladder inflammation.

stem: A 56-year-old female with suspected choledocholithiasis undergoes ERCP, which reveals biliary stones without bile duct wall thickening. Six hours after the procedure, she develops severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, associated with nausea and vomiting. Laboratory analysis shows serum lipase elevated to more than three times the upper limit of normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

opts.t: Acute pancreatitis related to ERCP procedure

expl: Epigastric pain to the back with lipase >3× normal hours after ERCP = post-ERCP pancreatitis, the commonest ERCP complication.

stem: A 35-year-old female presents with signs and symptoms of acute pancreatitis. Abdominal ultrasound reveals gallstones and a dilated common bile duct, consistent with biliary obstruction. There is no gallbladder wall thickening, no pericholecystic fluid, and no evidence of acute cholangitis. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
expl: Source key A. Gallstone pancreatitis with a dilated CBD on US suggests a retained/obstructing stone → ERCP to clear the duct. (Without cholangitis, many surgeons first confirm with MRCP/EUS; ERCP is clearly indicated with cholangitis or persistent obstruction.)

why.B: Diagnostic alternative when the stone is uncertain.

stem: A 95-year-old patient with a poor ASA score and multiple comorbidities presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever, and signs of acute cholecystitis. Imaging confirms gallbladder stones, gallbladder wall thickening, and pericholecystic fluid with a normal common bile duct (CBD). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?( same idea)
srcNote: Source note (Final 434 F Q13 (p. 171)): The related recall describes a burn patient in the ICU with RUQ pain, a thickened gallbladder, minimal pericholecystic fluid and no stones. It gives D. Cholecystostomy tube placement. Answer: D.
expl: Acute cholecystitis in a 95-year-old with a poor ASA and multiple comorbidities → percutaneous cholecystostomy (source control under local) ± antibiotics; cholecystectomy later if fit.

why.E: May fail; drainage is needed with pericholecystic fluid.

stem: What is the most common cause of acute pancreatitis?
expl: Gallstones are the commonest cause of acute pancreatitis worldwide (alcohol second).

stem: Prophylactic cholecystectomy?
srcNote: Incomplete recall: only one answer choice is supplied in the source.
expl: Prophylactic cholecystectomy is indicated for gallbladder polyps ≥1 cm (or growing), porcelain gallbladder, large stones >3 cm, and some high-risk groups (e.g. sickle cell on other surgery).

stem: 45 year old female presented with severe epigastric pain in the hypochondrium, mild icterus, febrile, leukocytosis. What's the best next step to confirm diagnosis
srcNote: (Gallstone related disorders)
expl: Fever, leukocytosis, upper abdominal pain and mild icterus → biliary pathology (cholecystitis/cholangitis) → ultrasound is the first and best test.

stem: A 50-year-old female presents with abdominal pain, vomiting and distension and increased bowel sound. Plain abdominal X-ray shows multiple air-fluid levels, a rounded opacity on the right side and air within the biliary tract. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Rigler's triad: small-bowel obstruction + pneumobilia + an ectopic (rounded) gallstone = gallstone ileus.

stem: 70 old female patient came to ER has signs of obstructive jaundice without fever or high wbc, US showed distended gallbladder 2 cm dilation of CBD and Intrahepatic duct dilation
srcNote: (Gallstone related disorders) Unanswered source question: the answer line names only the topic and gives no correct option. Incomplete stem and choice set: the source omits an explicit question sentence and records option D as "??".
expl: No key in the source. An elderly patient with painless obstructive jaundice, a distended gallbladder and a 2-cm CBD suggests a malignant distal obstruction → contrast-enhanced CT (pancreatic protocol) to find and stage the cause before any ERCP.

why.A: Therapeutic; done after CT (or for cholangitis).
why.B: Good for anatomy, but CT stages malignancy.

stem: A 45 y/o woman presented to the ER with painless jaundice, pale stool and dark urine. Labs showed an obstructive pattern. US revealed dilated gallbladder, 3cm diameter of the cystic duct, and intrahepatic biliary dilation. Which of the following is the best next step?
srcNote: (Gallstone related disorders) Unanswered source question: the answer line names only the topic and gives no correct option. Incomplete choice set: option D is blank in the source.
expl: No key in the source. Painless obstructive jaundice in a 45-year-old with a markedly dilated duct and intrahepatic dilatation → MRCP to define the biliary anatomy (choledochal cyst, stones, stricture) non-invasively before intervention.

why.C: Oral contrast isn't helpful for the bile ducts.

stem: A 67-year-old man presented with a history of yellowish discoloration of sclera and skin with dark urine and pale stool for one month. On examination he was jaundiced with palpable distended gallbladder. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this condition?
srcNote: (Hepato-bilio-pancreatic neoplasms) Source note (Final 427 F Q56 (p. 316)): Courvoisier’s sign (or law) describes an enlarged, palpable gallbladder in patients with obstructive jaundice caused by tumors of the biliary tree or by pancreatic head tumors.
expl: Painless progressive obstructive jaundice in an elderly man with a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier) = malignant distal obstruction → carcinoma of the pancreatic head.

why.A: Gallbladder is usually fibrosed/not palpable; painful, fluctuating jaundice.
why.B: Hilar tumour — gallbladder collapsed, not palpable.
why.D: Stone in the gallbladder neck compressing the CHD — pain, gallbladder not distended.

stem: A 70-year-old man with progressive painless jaundice, vitally stable, is referred to your clinic. You order liver function tests that showed an abnormal pattern consistent with obstruction, What is the next step in the management of this patient?
srcNote: ( Gallstone related disorders) Conflicting source versions: the retained version offers and keys ERCP; the 436 B version replaces this option with MRCP and keys it instead. Other source key (Final 436 B Q6): C. MRCP. Ans. C. Source note (Final 436 A Q12): Answer: A If fever was in the scenario then A is the answer (cholangitis). But if it's just a CBD stone do US is still not diagnostic do MCRP then do ERCP
expl: Source key C. Painless progressive obstructive jaundice in an elderly man → the source versions differ; ERCP (diagnostic brushing + stenting) was keyed. Many would image first with US/CT.

stem: A 28-year-old woman who is known to have multiple small gallstones, presented to the ER complaining of severe epigastric pain associated with vomiting for 18 hours. Physical examination revealed upper abdominal tenderness. Blood pressure 120/65 mmHg Heart rate 86 /min Temperature 37.8 Respiratory rate 18/min Test Result: (Normal value) WBC 13.4 (4-10.5 x 10 9 L) Serum amylase 5.4 (0.54-2.02 nkat/L) Alkaline phosphatase 3.2 (0.7-1.9 ukat/L) Total bilirubin 34 (3.5-16.5 umol/L) Direct bilirubin 19 (1.5-6.5 umol/L) Which of the following is the appropriate initial management?
srcNote: ? (Gallstone related disorders, Acute and chronic pancreatitis) Uncertain source key: the original answer includes a question mark.
expl: Source key C (marked "?"). Gallstone pancreatitis without cholangitis (stable, no fever, mild cholestasis) → initial management is IV crystalloid resuscitation; ERCP only if cholangitis/persistent obstruction; US to confirm the cause.

stem: A 45 year old female was admitted as a diagnosis of acute cholecystitis. Which of the following symptoms is associated with charcot's triad in diagnosis of acute cholangitis?
srcNote: (Acute abdomen)
expl: Source key B. Charcot's triad is fever, RUQ pain and jaundice; of the options, pruritus is the one that accompanies cholestatic jaundice.

stem: Patient presented with cholecytsitis complicated by choledolithaisis. What is the management?
srcNote: (acute abdomen)
expl: Cholecystitis with CBD stones → clear the CBD with ERCP and remove the gallbladder (same admission).

stem: Female pt with a history of RUQ colicky pain for 5 days and slight fever, they gave her 1L of 0.9 NS but she did not improve. What is the most likely dx of the pt?
srcNote: (Gallstone related disorders)
expl: RUQ colicky pain for days with fever not settling = acute cholecystitis (colic settles within hours; cholangitis needs jaundice).

stem: Patient presented through the emergency department complaining of right upper quadrant abdominal pain with jaundice yellow discoloration of sclera and dark urine and vomiting for 6 days and fever temperature (39.6) and US revealing intrahepatic and extrahepatic dilatation of biliary tree what is the most effective initial treatment?
srcNote: Ascending cholangitis, The pt has been vomiting for 6 days so we should replace fluids first.
expl: Six days of vomiting + sepsis (cholangitis) → first restore volume with IV fluids, then antibiotics and ERCP.

why.A: Essential too, but fluid resuscitation first in a dehydrated septic patient.

stem: 65-year-old patient with upper GI bleeding and jaundice. He has a history of liver resection for hemangioma 2 years ago. He had a recent road traffic accident. Ultrasound shows gallstones. There is bleeding from the ampulla of vater. Which of the following is most likely the cause for hemobilia in this patient?
srcNote: (answer is confirmed when Q was reviewed with the course organiser).
expl: Bleeding from the ampulla with jaundice after a recent road traffic accident = traumatic haemobilia (Quincke's triad: RUQ pain, jaundice, GI bleeding). Confirmed by the course organiser.

why.B: A rare cause of haemobilia, but trauma fits the history.

stem: 33-year-old women presented to the ER complaining of right upper quadrant pain for 8 days associated with fever, nausea and vomiting. Physical examination revealed marked tenderness in the right upper quadrant area of the abdomen. Blood pressure 115/56 mmHg Heart rate 83 /min Temperature 38.2 Respiratory rate 17/min Test Result Normal value WBC 16.5x109/L (4-10.5x109/L) US: thick wall of the gallbladder, pericholecystic fluid and multiple gallstones. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
srcNote: (Gallstone related disorders, Obstruction & Liver Masses) Source note (Final Year not stated Q34 (p. 265)): The related four-day presentation offers B. Non-interventional management. Answer: b.
expl: Source key B. Acute cholecystitis presenting late (8 days) is past the ideal early window — the classic answer is antibiotics now and delayed (interval) cholecystectomy. The doctor favours early surgery when presenting within the window.

why.A: Not a standard term (cholecystostomy is for unfit patients).

stem: What is the most specific and sensitive imaging modality to diagnose acute cholecystitis ?
srcNote: (Acute abdomen)
expl: Source key C — ultrasound is the first-line and most practical test. (Strictly, HIDA scan is the most sensitive and specific test for acute cholecystitis.)

why.B: Actually the most sensitive/specific, but not keyed.

stem: A 45 year old obese woman who is known to have cholelithiasis, presents to the emergency room complaining of severe continuous mid-abdominal pain associated with nausea and vomiting for 16 hours. On examination, she has a low-grade fever with epigastric tenderness. Laboratory values showed: WBC count: 12.000 (4.000-10.000/ml) and serum amylase 2000 mmol/1 (23-125). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: (Acute and chronic pancreatitis)
expl: Known gallstones + continuous epigastric/mid-abdominal pain with vomiting = acute (biliary) pancreatitis.

stem: A 43 year old obese woman presents to ER with severe epigastric pain that started after a heavy meal. She has had several milder episodes before related to fatty food consumption. Physical exam reveals tenderness in the right subcostal area. Which of the following hormones likely provoked the current attack?
expl: Fatty food → duodenal I-cells release CCK → gallbladder contraction pushes stones into the cystic duct → biliary colic.

stem: Which one of the following represent 'Charcot's triad in acute cholangitis?

opts.t: Right upper quadrant pain, fever and vomiting
Right upper quadrant pain with tenderness and fever
Right upper quadrant pain, fever and hypotension
Right upper quadrant pain, fever and jaundice

expl: Charcot's triad = RUQ pain, fever and jaundice.

stem: Which of the following is a complication of obesity surgery?
srcNote: (Upper gastrointestinal and bariatric surgery, abdominal wall, umbilicus, herniae, and retroperitoneum), This is because as the body metabolises fat during rapid Weight Loss, it causes the liver to secrete extra cholesterol into the bile, potentially causing gallstones.
expl: Rapid weight loss after bariatric surgery raises biliary cholesterol → gallstones. Diabetes, hypertension and hypothyroidism improve or aren't caused.

stem: Which ONE of the following represents Courvoisier's law in a 75-year-old patient with obstructive jaundice?

opts.t: Gallbladder is palpable the jaundice is unlikely to be due to stone
Gallbladder is palpable the jaundice is due to common bile duct stone
Gallbladder is not palpable the jaundice is due to common hepatic stone
Gallbladder is not palpable the jaundice is due to pancreatic

srcNote: (Gallstone related disorders) Incomplete option D: the source wording ends at "pancreatic".
expl: Courvoisier's law: in a jaundiced patient a palpable gallbladder is unlikely to be due to stones (chronic cholecystitis makes the gallbladder fibrotic and non-distensible) → suspect malignancy (pancreatic head/periampullary).

stem: A 60 year old man presented with a history of jaundice, itching and weight loss for 6 months. Laboratory values showed evidence of direct hyperbilirubinemia. Which of the following is the appropriate next step for diagnosis?
srcNote: Conflicting source keys: the retained version gives abdominal CT; the undated version of the same case gives ultrasound. Other source key (Final Year not stated Q31 (p. 264)): A. Ultrasound abdomen. Answer: a.
expl: Painless jaundice with weight loss in an older man = malignancy until proven otherwise → contrast CT (the undated version keyed US first).

stem: air in biliary tree:
srcNote: Incomplete recall with different source choices: the retained version gives pneumobilia; the final-exam version gives gallstone ileus among two options. Other source key (Final 427 F Q57 (p. 316)): A. Gallstone ileus; B. Paralytic ileus. Answer: A.
expl: Air in the biliary tree = pneumobilia (after sphincterotomy, biliary-enteric anastomosis, or a gallstone fistula — gallstone ileus).

stem: Acalculous cholecystitis

opts.t: CT scan is the investigation of choice
Happen usually to ill pt because of another condition
Accounts for 5-10% of the cholecystitis (it is written in Loran’s 20%)

srcNote: Incomplete stem: the source does not specify whether it asks for a correct or incorrect statement. Its original options and key are preserved.
expl: Incomplete stem — it asks for the incorrect statement. Acalculous cholecystitis happens in critically ill patients (burns, ICU, sepsis), makes up 5–10% of cholecystitis and has an aggressive course (gangrene, perforation). US (± HIDA) — not CT — is first-line.

stem: ERCP NOT done in “incomplete Q”
srcNote: Incomplete recall: only one choice is supplied. The original source image is included below.
expl: ERCP needs endoscopic access to the papilla; after gastrectomy with Billroth II/Roux-en-Y reconstruction, the papilla is hard or impossible to reach.

stem: Bile flow
srcNote: Source key was A; corrected — see explanation. Incomplete recall: no time interval is stated. The source prints "mg" in option A and "ml" in option B; its original wording and key are preserved.
expl: The liver secretes about 500–1000 mL of bile a day (the doctor quotes ~1–1.5 L); 300–500 is too low (and "mg" is a unit error in the source).

stem: Jaundice least adversely affect which of these?
srcNote: Incomplete choice set: only three options are provided in the source. Year not stated
expl: Source key A. Jaundice mainly affects the skin (pruritus), urine and stool colour; yellow vision (xanthopsia) is rare. The recall is unreliable — hearing is not affected by jaundice at all.

stem: Another similar question to the previous one came.. But in the scenario they said US was done and showed dilated intra hepatic and extra hepatic duct so what is the investigation of choice that lead you to the diagnosis?
srcNote: Incomplete recall: the stem refers to the preceding source question, and only three choices are supplied. Source note (Final Year not stated Q31 (p. 264)): Preceding source scenario: A 60-year-old male presented with history of jaundice, itching and weight loss for 6 months. Laboratory values showed evidence of direct hyperbilirubinemia.
expl: Source key A. With US showing dilated intra- and extrahepatic ducts, CT abdomen identifies the level and cause of obstruction (mass, stones) and stages malignancy; MRCP is the alternative for anatomy.
